name: Argentina
summary: Children, parents and a spouse are forced heirs: descendants are guaranteed two thirds, ascendants and a spouse one half (Civil and Commercial Code art. 2445). Argentine law applies to a person domiciled in Argentina, and to Argentine real estate whoever owns it, so a foreign resident cannot escape the reserved share by choosing another law. Argentina has a statutory trust (fideicomiso) but private-interest foundations are not allowed; foundations must pursue the common good.
reserved_share: Forced heirs (art. 2444): descendants, ascendants, spouse. Legítima: descendants 2/3, ascendants 1/2, spouse 1/2 of the estate (Código Civil y Comercial art. 2445). Lifetime gifts count toward the calculation and can be reduced (arts. 2386, 2453 ff.).
foreign_law_note: Succession is governed by the law of the deceased's last domicile (CCyC art. 2644); real estate located in Argentina is governed by Argentine law (art. 2643). No general right to choose the law of nationality was found. A resident foreigner is therefore under Argentine heirship rules for Argentine assets.
trust_note: Fideicomiso is regulated in CCyC arts. 1666-1707 (a trustee holds the assets for beneficiaries; it cannot be used to damage the legítima, art. 1700). Argentina is not a party to the Hague Trusts Convention, so foreign trusts are not recognised by treaty; the treatment of a foreign common-law trust is not settled in the sources found. Foundations (fundaciones, CCyC arts. 193-224 and Ley 19.836) must have a common-good purpose and no profit motive, so a family foundation is not available.
open_questions: How Argentine courts and the tax authority treat foreign common-law trusts (recognition and tax) was not sourced.
Whether a fideicomiso funded in life is protected from reduction for legítima beyond art. 1700 was not sourced; confirm with a local lawyer.
Whether Argentina reforms the Civil and Commercial Code succession rules (executive reform proposals) was not checked.
